steps.overview: This step gets n8n running so you have a working lab for the rest of the track. You will compare n8n Cloud with self-hosting, start n8n with npx or Docker, learn the editor layout, and understand how credentials are stored and encrypted. The Level 1 and Level 2 courses assume you can build and run workflows, and persistent storage is the first thing that breaks in real self-hosted setups.
objectives: Choose between n8n Cloud and self-hosting for a given team, budget and compliance need
Start n8n locally with npx n8n and with Docker, then open the editor on port 5678
Mount a persistent volume at /home/node/.n8n so workflows, credentials and the encryption key survive restarts
Navigate the editor: canvas, nodes, connections, the node panel and the Executions list
Explain how n8n stores and encrypts credentials, and what happens if the encryption key is lost

concepts.explanation: A hosted service run by n8n. It handles updates, backups, scaling and HTTPS, and offers a free trial before you pick a paid plan. Choose it when you want no server work. Your data then sits on n8n's infrastructure.

You run n8n on your own laptop, VM or Kubernetes cluster under n8n's Sustainable Use License. It is free for internal business use. You are responsible for updates, backups, security, SSL and uptime. Choose it for data residency, custom nodes or cost control at high volume.

Downloads and runs n8n using Node.js, with no permanent install. It needs a Node.js version that n8n currently supports, so check the docs. Data goes to ~/.n8n in your home folder. It is good for quick tests. Docker is preferred for anything longer-lived.

Inside the official image, n8n keeps its data in /home/node/.n8n. That data includes the SQLite database, the config file holding the encryption key, and binary data. If you do not mount a volume there, removing the container deletes everything. A named volume (e.g. n8n_data) keeps that data on the host.

The canvas is where you build a workflow. Nodes are the steps: trigger nodes start a workflow, and action or core nodes process data. Connections are the lines that pass items, an array of JSON objects, from one node's output to the next node's input.

Each workflow run is an execution. It shows the data in and out of every node, and whether the run succeeded or failed. Manual test runs from the editor differ from production runs, which fire from an active or published workflow's trigger. The Executions list is your first debugging tool.

Credentials are saved login details, such as API keys and OAuth tokens. They are stored separately from workflows, and nodes refer to them by ID. n8n encrypts credentials in the database with an encryption key. Exporting a workflow does not include the credential secrets.

On first start, n8n generates a random key and saves it in the config file inside ~/.n8n. You can also set it yourself with the N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY environment variable. If you lose or change the key, saved credentials can no longer be decrypted. Every instance that shares one database, such as queue-mode workers, must use the same key.

keyFacts: The default editor and webhook port is 5678, so the editor opens at http://localhost:5678.
Official image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n (also n8nio/n8n on Docker Hub).
The data directory inside the container is /home/node/.n8n. Mount your volume exactly there.
The default database is SQLite. PostgreSQL is the recommended choice for production (DB_TYPE=postgresdb plus the DB_POSTGRESDB_* variables).
Credentials are encrypted at rest. Keep the encryption key in a safe place and back it up along with the database.
Set GENERIC_TIMEZONE (and TZ) so Schedule triggers fire in your timezone, for example Asia/Kolkata.
Behind a reverse proxy or a public domain, set WEBHOOK_URL so webhook URLs show the correct public address.
The first time you open a fresh self-hosted instance, you create the owner account.

example.caption: docker-compose.yml: n8n with a persistent named volume (start with docker compose up -d)
example.code:
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
    container_name: n8n
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"
    environment:
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata
      - TZ=Asia/Kolkata
      # Optional: pin the key so credentials stay readable if config is lost
      # - N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=change-me-long-random-string
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n

volumes:
  n8n_data:

# Quick one-liner equivalent:
# docker volume create n8n_data
# docker run -it --rm --name n8n -p 5678:5678 \
#   -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n

pitfalls: Running docker run --rm without a -v mount. All workflows and credentials disappear when the container stops.
Mounting the volume to the wrong path, such as /root/.n8n or /data, instead of /home/node/.n8n.
Recreating the instance on an empty volume, or with a different N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, while pointing at an old database. The old credentials then fail to decrypt.
Thinking an exported workflow JSON contains your API keys. It does not, so credentials must be recreated or migrated separately.
Confusing test executions with production executions. A webhook's test URL only listens while you are actively testing in the editor.
Using SQLite on a busy production server, or skipping backups, because self-hosting makes you the person responsible for operations.

workflow.title: Hands-on: run n8n in Docker and prove persistence

steps.label: Install and verify Docker
steps.detail: Install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine, then run docker --version to confirm it works.

steps.label: Create a named volume
steps.detail: Run docker volume create n8n_data, or let the compose file create it.

steps.label: Start the n8n container
steps.detail: Run docker compose up -d with the volume mounted at /home/node/.n8n and port 5678 published.

steps.label: Create the owner account
steps.detail: Open http://localhost:5678 and set up the owner user.

steps.label: Build and save a workflow
steps.detail: Add a Manual Trigger and an Edit Fields (Set) node, add a test credential, save, then run it and check Executions.

steps.label: Restart the container
steps.detail: Run docker compose down then docker compose up -d, which removes and recreates the container but keeps the volume.

steps.label: Verify the checkpoint
steps.detail: Log in again and confirm the workflow, the credential and the past executions are all still present.

objective.question: You start n8n on your laptop with default settings. Which URL opens the editor?
options: http://localhost:5678
http://localhost:443
http://localhost:3000
http://localhost:8080
objective.explanation: 5678 is n8n's default port for both the editor and webhooks. 8080, 3000 and 443 are common ports for other tools, not n8n defaults.

objective.question: You run the official n8n Docker image. At which path inside the container must you mount a volume so that workflows and credentials persist?
options: /home/node/.n8n
/root/.n8n
/data
/var/lib/n8n
objective.explanation: The n8n data directory inside the container is /home/node/.n8n, because the container runs as the node user. The other paths are not where n8n keeps its data.

objective.question: A learner runs `docker run -it --rm -p 5678:5678 docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n`, builds two workflows, stops the container and starts it again. Both workflows are gone. What is the most likely cause?
options: The workflows were never activated
Port 5678 was already in use
No volume was mounted at /home/node/.n8n, so the data was lost with the container
The SQLite database was corrupted when the container stopped
objective.explanation: With no volume, the SQLite database lives in the container's writable layer, and --rm deletes that layer when the container stops. Activation and port conflicts do not delete saved workflows.

objective.question: Which image reference is the official n8n Docker image?
options: ghcr.io/n8n/n8n-server
docker.io/library/n8n
n8n/official
docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
objective.explanation: The official image is docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n, also published as n8nio/n8n on Docker Hub. The other names are not official n8n images.

objective.question: You install n8n without any database settings. Which database does it use?
options: MySQL
MongoDB
SQLite
PostgreSQL
objective.explanation: SQLite is the default. It stores everything in a file inside the n8n data directory. PostgreSQL is supported but must be configured. MongoDB is not a supported database for n8n.

objective.question: Your team is moving a self-hosted n8n instance to production and wants to use PostgreSQL. Which configuration is correct?
options: DB_TYPE=postgresdb plus the DB_POSTGRESDB_* variables (host, port, database, user, password)
N8N_DATABASE=postgresql plus PG_HOST
Mount a PostgreSQL volume at /home/node/.n8n
DB_TYPE=postgres plus DATABASE_URL
objective.explanation: n8n expects DB_TYPE=postgresdb, with connection details in variables such as DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST, DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE, DB_POSTGRESDB_USER and DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD. The other variable names are not n8n's, and a volume mount does not change the database type.

objective.question: You copy an n8n database to a new server and start a fresh n8n container with a new, empty data volume. Workflows load fine, but every node using a saved credential fails with a decryption error. What went wrong?
options: The new instance uses a different encryption key from the one that encrypted the credentials
Credentials are never stored in the database
The owner account was not recreated
PostgreSQL does not support encrypted credentials
objective.explanation: Credentials are encrypted at rest with the instance's encryption key. A new instance with no N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY generates a new random key, so it cannot decrypt the old credentials. Set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY to the original key to fix this.

objective.question: A Schedule Trigger set for 9:00 AM fires at 2:30 PM IST on a self-hosted instance in Mumbai. What should you set?
options: N8N_PORT=Asia/Kolkata
DB_TIMEZONE=IST
GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata (and TZ=Asia/Kolkata)
WEBHOOK_URL=Asia/Kolkata
objective.explanation: Schedule triggers use GENERIC_TIMEZONE. Setting TZ as well keeps the container's system time consistent. A 5.5-hour gap means the instance was running on UTC. The other variables do not control schedule timing.

objective.question: n8n runs behind Nginx at https://automation.example.in, but the Webhook node still shows URLs starting with http://localhost:5678. What fixes this?
options: Switch the database to PostgreSQL
Recreate the webhook credentials
Change the container port to 443
Set WEBHOOK_URL=https://automation.example.in/
objective.explanation: Behind a reverse proxy, n8n cannot know its public address, so you set WEBHOOK_URL to tell it. Changing the port, the database or credentials does not affect the displayed webhook URL.

objective.question: You open a freshly installed self-hosted n8n instance in the browser for the first time. What happens?
options: You must enter an n8n Cloud licence key
The editor opens with no login at all, permanently
You are asked to create the owner account
You log in with admin/admin
objective.explanation: A fresh self-hosted instance asks you to set up the owner account. That account then manages the instance and its users. There is no default admin/admin login, and no Cloud licence is needed to start.

objective.question: A developer types `npx n8n` and gets 'command not found: npx'. What is missing?
options: Node.js (with npm, which provides npx)
An n8n Cloud account
A PostgreSQL server
Docker Desktop
objective.explanation: npx ships with npm, which is installed with Node.js. The npx route runs n8n directly on Node.js, so it needs neither Docker nor PostgreSQL nor a Cloud account.

objective.question: A workflow that ran overnight sent the wrong email to a customer. Where in the editor do you look first to see what data each node received and produced in that run?
options: The workflow's Executions list, opening that specific execution
The Templates library
The node's Settings tab
The Credentials page
objective.explanation: The Executions list keeps past runs. Opening one shows the input and output data of each node, which is how you debug production runs. Credentials, node settings and templates do not show run history.

objective.question: On the n8n canvas, what does a connection line between two nodes represent?
options: The path along which output items of one node are passed as input to the next
A database foreign key
A scheduled time dependency
A shared credential between the nodes
objective.explanation: Connections define data flow. Items output by one node become the input of the connected node. Credentials are attached to individual nodes, not to connections.

objective.question: A small marketing team has no one to manage servers, backups or upgrades, and wants to start building workflows today. Which option fits best?
options: n8n Cloud
Run `npx n8n` on one laptop for the whole team
Build n8n from source
Self-host on a VPS with PostgreSQL
objective.explanation: n8n Cloud is managed by n8n, so hosting, upgrades and infrastructure are handled for you. Self-hosting needs someone to own operations. A single laptop is not a reliable shared server.

objective.question: You never set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY on a self-hosted Docker instance. Which statement is true?
options: n8n generates a random key on first launch and saves it in the data directory (/home/node/.n8n), so losing that volume loses the key
The key is fetched from n8n Cloud at each start
n8n refuses to start
Credentials are stored in plain text
objective.explanation: n8n auto-generates a key and stores it in a config file in its data directory. Credentials are still encrypted. If that directory is lost or not persisted, the key is lost too, so it is safer to set and back up N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY yourself.

subjective.question: Compare n8n Cloud with self-hosting the Community Edition. How would you advise a client to choose?
subjective.answer: n8n Cloud is hosted and managed by n8n. You sign up, start a trial and build workflows right away. Hosting, upgrades, uptime and infrastructure are handled for you. Self-hosting means you run n8n yourself, with npx, Docker or Kubernetes. You get full control over data location, network access, environment variables and scaling, which helps with data-residency rules or internal-only systems. The cost is that you own the operations: the database, backups, the encryption key, TLS, the reverse proxy, upgrades and monitoring. My advice depends on two things: compliance and in-house ops skill. A team with no DevOps support should start on Cloud. A company with strict data policies, private-network integrations and engineers who can run containers can self-host, ideally with PostgreSQL in production. I would also check the licence terms for their use case.
keyPoints: Cloud is managed: fast start, no infrastructure to run
Self-hosted gives control over data, network and configuration
Self-hosting means owning backups, upgrades, security and the database
Decide on compliance needs and in-house ops capability

subjective.question: Write the Docker commands to run n8n with a persistent volume, and explain each part.
subjective.answer: First I create a named volume: `docker volume create n8n_data`. Then I run: `docker run -it --rm --name n8n -p 5678:5678 -e GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata -e TZ=Asia/Kolkata -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n`. The `-it` flag attaches an interactive terminal so I can see the logs. `--rm` removes the container when it stops, which is safe here because the data lives in the volume. `--name n8n` gives the container a readable name. `-p 5678:5678` maps the default editor and webhook port to my machine. The `-e` flags set the timezone so Schedule triggers fire at Indian time. `-v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n` is the critical part: it mounts the volume at n8n's data directory, where the SQLite database and the auto-generated encryption key live. The last argument is the official image. I then open http://localhost:5678 and create the owner account.
keyPoints: docker volume create, then -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n
-p 5678:5678 exposes the default port
--rm is safe only because the data is in the volume
Official image docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n; set the timezone variables

subjective.question: How would you prove that your n8n workflows survive a container restart?
subjective.answer: I would run a small, repeatable test. First, start the container with the volume mounted at /home/node/.n8n. Open the editor, create the owner account, build a simple workflow such as Manual Trigger to Set node, save it, and add one test credential. Run the workflow once so there is an execution in the history. Next, stop the container. If I used --rm, it is deleted completely, which is an even stronger test. Then I run the same docker run command with the same volume. When I log in, the owner account should still work without a new setup screen. The workflow, the credential and the execution history should all be present. The credential should also still decrypt; I can open it or run a node that uses it. Finally, `docker volume inspect n8n_data` confirms where the data lives. If the setup screen appears again, the mount path or volume name is wrong.
keyPoints: Create a workflow, a credential and an execution before the restart
Remove or restart the container, then reuse the same volume
The owner login still works and no setup screen appears
The credential still decrypts, which proves the encryption key persisted

subjective.question: Named volume or bind mount for /home/node/.n8n — which would you use and what problems can occur?
subjective.answer: Both work. A named volume, like `-v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n`, is managed by Docker. It is portable and avoids most permission problems, so it is my default. A bind mount, like `-v /srv/n8n:/home/node/.n8n`, maps a host folder. It is handy when I want to see the files directly or fit an existing host backup tool. The common problem with bind mounts is permissions. The container runs as the non-root node user, so the host folder must be writable by that user ID. Otherwise n8n fails to start or cannot write its database and config. Another mistake is mounting at the wrong path, such as /root/.n8n or /data. n8n then writes to the container layer and the data disappears on removal. Also avoid storing a busy SQLite file on network file systems, because file locking can be unreliable there.
keyPoints: A named volume is the simple, low-friction default
A bind mount gives direct host access but needs correct permissions
The container runs as the node user, not root
A wrong mount path silently loses data

subjective.question: When is SQLite fine for n8n, and when would you move to PostgreSQL?
subjective.answer: SQLite is the default. It is a single file in the data directory and needs no setup, so it is ideal for learning, local development and small personal instances with modest load. For production I would move to PostgreSQL, which n8n recommends. PostgreSQL handles concurrent writes better, which matters when many executions save data at the same time. It supports proper backup tooling and point-in-time recovery. It runs as a separate managed service, so the n8n container stays stateless apart from the encryption key. It is also needed for scaled setups such as queue mode with multiple workers. To configure it I set DB_TYPE=postgresdb and the DB_POSTGRESDB_* variables: host, port, database, user, password and schema if needed. I decide this early, because moving existing data between databases later takes extra effort.
keyPoints: SQLite is zero-config and good for dev and small use
PostgreSQL is recommended for production
Better concurrency, backups and multi-instance scaling
Configure with DB_TYPE=postgresdb and DB_POSTGRESDB_*

subjective.question: Explain how n8n stores credentials and why the encryption key is so important.
subjective.answer: When I save a credential, such as an API key or OAuth token, n8n encrypts it and stores it in its database, SQLite or PostgreSQL. Nodes refer to the credential and never hold the secret in the workflow JSON. So exporting or sharing a workflow does not leak the secret. The encryption uses the instance's encryption key. If N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not set, n8n generates a random key on first launch and saves it in the data directory. The key and the database are a pair. If you restore the database on a new instance with a different key, every credential fails to decrypt and has to be re-entered. For any serious deployment I set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY explicitly from a secret store. I back it up separately and securely, and I use the same value on every instance or worker that shares the database.
keyPoints: Credentials are encrypted at rest in the database
Workflows reference credentials; secrets are not embedded in the workflow
The key is auto-generated into the data directory if not set
Back up the key with the database; reuse it across instances

subjective.question: Design a backup and restore plan for a self-hosted n8n instance.
subjective.answer: There are two things to protect: the database and the encryption key. With SQLite, both live in the /home/node/.n8n volume. I back up that volume regularly, ideally while n8n is stopped or using a consistent snapshot, so the SQLite file is not caught mid-write. With PostgreSQL, I use pg_dump or managed snapshots for the database, and I keep N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY in a secrets manager or vault. As an extra safety net, I can export workflows and keep them in Git, though exports do not replace a database backup. I store backups off the server and test restores regularly. A restore means: start the same n8n version, point it at the restored database or volume, set the same encryption key, then check that credentials decrypt and triggers work. An untested backup is only a hope.
keyPoints: Back up both the database and the encryption key
SQLite: snapshot the volume consistently; Postgres: pg_dump or snapshots
Store backups off the server; workflow exports in Git are extra
Test restores: same key, check that credentials decrypt

subjective.question: Your Schedule Trigger fires at the wrong time on a Docker deployment. Explain the cause and the fix.
subjective.answer: Containers usually default to UTC. A workflow scheduled for 9:00 then runs at 9:00 UTC, which is 2:30 PM in India. n8n's Schedule Trigger uses the instance timezone from GENERIC_TIMEZONE. The fix is to set GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata. I also set TZ=Asia/Kolkata so the container's system time, logs and date functions agree. Then I recreate the container with the same volume. Individual workflows can also override the timezone in workflow settings, which helps when one instance serves teams in different regions. After the change, I check the next run times and confirm with a test execution. IST has no daylight saving, but for clients in Europe or the US, using a named zone rather than a fixed offset makes DST shifts automatic.
keyPoints: Containers default to UTC
GENERIC_TIMEZONE controls the Schedule Trigger; also set TZ
A per-workflow timezone setting can override it
Use named zones like Asia/Kolkata and verify after the change

subjective.question: Why do you need WEBHOOK_URL when n8n runs behind a reverse proxy?
subjective.answer: Inside the container, n8n only knows it is listening on port 5678. Behind Nginx, Traefik or Caddy with a domain and TLS, the public address is something like https://automation.example.in. Without being told, n8n builds webhook URLs from its internal view, so the Webhook node shows http://localhost:5678/webhook/... External services like Stripe, GitHub or a form tool cannot reach that. OAuth redirect URLs can break for the same reason. Setting WEBHOOK_URL=https://automation.example.in/ makes n8n display and register the correct public URL. I also make sure the proxy forwards the right headers and supports the editor's live connection, and that TLS ends correctly at the proxy. After the change, I copy the production webhook URL and test it from outside the network.
keyPoints: n8n cannot infer its public address behind a proxy
Without it, webhook URLs show localhost:5678
Set WEBHOOK_URL to the public https domain
Test from outside; OAuth callbacks depend on it too

subjective.question: Describe the main parts of the n8n editor to a new team member.
subjective.answer: The canvas is the workspace where you build a workflow visually. Each box is a node, a single step. Every workflow starts with a trigger node, such as a Manual Trigger, Schedule Trigger or Webhook, which decides when the workflow runs. Action nodes then do the work: call an API, transform data, branch with IF, or send a message. Connections are the lines between nodes. They carry data, as a list of items, from one node's output to the next node's input. Opening a node shows its parameters, its input and output data, and its credential selection. You can run the whole workflow or test a single step and see the data immediately. The Executions tab lists past runs, both test runs and production runs, so you can inspect what happened. Credentials are managed separately and selected inside nodes.
keyPoints: Canvas is the visual workspace; nodes are steps
Trigger nodes start workflows; action nodes do the work
Connections pass items from output to input
Node panel shows parameters and data; Executions show history

subjective.question: How do you use the Executions view to debug a failed production run?
subjective.answer: I open the workflow's Executions list, or the instance-wide one, and filter for failed runs. Opening a failed execution shows the workflow as it ran. The failing node is highlighted, and I can click each node to see its exact input and output items and the error message. Usually the cause is clear from the data: a missing field, an unexpected API response, an expired credential, or a rate limit. If the error depends on that specific data, I can copy it into the editor, or pin data on the trigger, and rerun the workflow while I fix it. This avoids waiting for the real event to happen again. I also check how the instance saves execution data. If successful or failed runs are not being saved, there will be nothing to inspect. Very large histories can also bloat the database, so pruning settings matter.
keyPoints: Filter Executions for failed runs
Inspect per-node input, output and the error message
Reuse that execution's data to reproduce the issue in the editor
Execution saving and pruning settings affect what is available

subjective.question: Compare running n8n with `npx n8n` and with Docker for local work.
subjective.answer: `npx n8n` downloads and runs n8n on the Node.js already installed on your machine. It is the quickest way to try n8n if Node.js is installed. Data goes into the .n8n folder in your home directory, so it persists between runs. The downsides: you depend on a compatible Node.js version, and the environment differs from how production usually runs. Docker packages n8n with its own runtime in the official image docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n. It does not touch your Node.js install, and it behaves the same on every machine. It also matches common production deployments, so environment variables, volumes and upgrades work the same way locally and on a server. The catch is that you must mount a volume at /home/node/.n8n, or data is lost. For quick learning, npx is fine. For anything I will deploy later, I use Docker from day one.
keyPoints: npx needs a compatible Node.js; data goes in ~/.n8n
Docker gives an isolated, reproducible runtime
Docker matches production patterns: env vars, volumes, upgrades
Docker needs a volume at /home/node/.n8n to persist data

subjective.question: How would you upgrade a Docker-based n8n instance safely?
subjective.answer: First, I back up the data volume or the PostgreSQL database, and confirm the encryption key is stored safely. Then I read the release notes for breaking changes, especially on major versions, which can change behaviour or defaults. In production I pin a specific image tag rather than using latest, so upgrades are deliberate and repeatable. The upgrade itself: pull the new image tag, stop and remove the old container, and start a new one with the same volume, environment variables and encryption key. n8n runs any database migrations on startup, so I watch the logs. Afterwards, I check that I can log in, credentials decrypt, active workflows and triggers are running, and webhooks respond. If something breaks, I roll back to the previous tag and restore the backup, because migrations may not reverse cleanly. I try it on a staging copy first where possible.
keyPoints: Back up the database or volume and the key first
Pin image versions; read the release notes
Recreate the container with the same volume, env vars and key; watch migrations
Verify afterwards; keep a rollback path

subjective.question: What security steps would you take when first setting up a self-hosted n8n instance that will be reachable from the internet?
subjective.answer: First, I create the owner account immediately. A fresh instance shows the setup screen, and I do not want anyone else to claim it. I use a strong password and enable two-factor authentication if available. I do not expose port 5678 directly. I put n8n behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS on a proper domain, set WEBHOOK_URL to that domain, and limit firewall access to the proxy. I set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY explicitly from a secret store, not in a file that gets committed to Git, and I keep a backup of it. I use PostgreSQL with its own strong credentials and do not expose the database to the internet. I keep the image updated with security releases. I also follow least privilege: give API credentials only the scopes workflows need, and invite other users with suitable roles rather than sharing the owner login.
keyPoints: Create the owner account immediately with a strong password
Use HTTPS via a reverse proxy; do not expose 5678 directly
Set and protect N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY; keep the database private
Keep n8n updated; use least-privilege credentials and user roles

subjective.question: After a colleague migrates n8n to a new server, workflows appear but every credential throws an error. Walk through your troubleshooting.
subjective.answer: Workflows loading means the database moved correctly. Credentials failing almost always points to the encryption key. I would check the logs first; a decryption error confirms it. Next, I check whether the old server had N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY set. If not, the key was auto-generated and stored in a config file inside the old /home/node/.n8n directory. If only the database was copied, with a fresh data volume, the new instance generated a new key. The fix is to get the original key, from the old config file or the secret store, and set it as N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY on the new instance. Then I restart and test a credential. If the original key is truly lost, the credentials cannot be recovered, and each one must be re-entered by hand. Going forward, I would document the key in a vault and add it to the migration checklist.
keyPoints: Workflows loading but credentials failing points to a key mismatch
An auto-generated key lives in the old data directory's config
Set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY to the original value and restart
A lost key means re-entering credentials; document the key in future

steps.overview: This step teaches how every n8n workflow starts (triggers) and the core nodes that move and shape data: HTTP Request, Edit Fields (Set), IF, Switch and Merge. You will also learn to pin data for fast testing and to activate (publish) a workflow so it runs without the editor open. The Level 1 and Level 2 knowledge checks test these topics, and every real automation depends on them.
objectives: Choose the right trigger (Manual, Schedule, Webhook or app trigger) for a given use case and explain test vs production behaviour
Call any REST API with the HTTP Request node, including authentication and query parameters
Reshape, route and combine items using Edit Fields (Set), IF, Switch and Merge
Pin node output to test downstream nodes without re-calling external APIs
Activate a scheduled workflow and confirm it ran by checking the Executions list

concepts.explanation: The first node in a workflow. It decides when the workflow starts. A workflow that runs on its own needs at least one non-manual trigger, such as Schedule, Webhook or an app trigger. Nodes after the trigger are action or core nodes.
Starts the workflow only when you click the test button in the editor. It is for building and debugging. It never fires in production, so a workflow with only a Manual Trigger cannot run on its own.

Runs the workflow at fixed intervals (seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months) or on a custom cron expression. It only fires when the workflow is active or published. It uses the workflow timezone from Workflow Settings, or the instance default if none is set.

Gives the workflow an HTTP endpoint that external systems can call. It has a Test URL, which listens only while you wait for a test event in the editor, and a Production URL, which works only when the workflow is active. Response mode can be Immediately, When Last Node Finishes, or Using 'Respond to Webhook' node.

Service-specific triggers, such as Gmail Trigger, Google Sheets Trigger or Telegram Trigger. They start a workflow when an event happens in that app. Some register a webhook with the service. Others poll the service at an interval you set.

Data moves between nodes as an array of items, and each item holds a json object (plus optional binary data). Most nodes run once for each incoming item. If an HTTP Request receives 5 items, it makes 5 calls unless you design it otherwise.

Calls any REST API with GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and other methods. It supports predefined credential types or generic auth (Header, Basic, OAuth2, Query). It also offers query parameters, headers, body, pagination and batching. You can import a cURL command to fill the node quickly.

Adds, renames or overwrites fields on each item. It has Manual Mapping mode and JSON mode. The 'Include Other Input Fields' option controls whether the original fields are kept. Use it to build a clean summary object before you send a message.

IF checks conditions and sends items to a true output or a false output. Switch routes items to many outputs, using Rules or an Expression, with an optional fallback output. Merge joins branches by Append, Combine (by matching fields, by position or all combinations), SQL Query or Choose Branch.

Pinning freezes a node's output so that later test runs reuse it instead of calling the API again. Pinned data is used only in manual (test) executions and is ignored in production runs. You cannot pin output that contains binary data.

keyFacts: Manual Trigger never runs in production; you need Schedule, Webhook or an app trigger for unattended runs.
Webhook Test URL works only while the editor is listening for a test event. The Production URL works only when the workflow is active (published).
The Test URL and Production URL are different. A common bug is giving the Test URL to an external system.
Schedule Trigger uses the workflow timezone from Workflow Settings, or the instance timezone (GENERIC_TIMEZONE on self-hosted). Set it to Asia/Kolkata if you expect IST.
After you change a schedule, save the workflow and publish it again; unsaved trigger changes do not apply to production.
Nodes run once per input item by default. Use Edit Fields, Aggregate or Code nodes when you need a single combined summary.
IF has exactly two outputs (true/false). Switch has many outputs and an optional fallback output.
Pinned data affects test runs only; production executions always fetch live data.
Production executions appear in the Executions list. Use it to prove that a scheduled run happened.
In newer n8n versions the 'Active' toggle became a Publish action. The concept is the same: only an activated or published version runs on triggers.

example.caption: Importable workflow: weekday 8 AM IST weather fetch, summary built with Edit Fields, sent by Gmail

pitfalls: Testing with the Manual Trigger and then assuming the workflow will run on its own. Add a Schedule Trigger and activate (publish) the workflow.
Forgetting the timezone. The schedule fires at 8 AM in the instance timezone, for example America/New_York, instead of 8 AM IST.
Leaving data pinned and believing production uses it. Pinned data is ignored in production, so live API errors can still appear there.
Sending one email per item. An API that returns 20 items gives 20 messages unless you aggregate first or set the node to execute once.
Mixing up IF and Switch, or Merge modes. Combine 'by matching fields' needs a common key, while Append simply stacks items from both inputs.
Using the Webhook Test URL in another system's settings. It stops working once you leave the editor.

objective.question: You built a workflow that starts with a Manual Trigger. It fetches sales data and emails a report. You publish the workflow and expect a report every morning. Nothing arrives. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Manual Trigger needs a cron expression to run in production
The email node must be pinned before production runs
Manual Trigger workflows run only on n8n Cloud, not self-hosted
The Manual Trigger runs only when you click to execute it in the editor, so it never fires unattended
objective.explanation: The Manual Trigger exists only for testing in the editor and never runs in production. For unattended runs you need a Schedule Trigger, a Webhook or an app trigger. The other options describe features that do not exist.

objective.question: A developer tests a Webhook node, copies the URL shown in the node and gives it to a payment provider. Calls work during testing. The next day every call from the provider fails. What is the most likely reason?
options: Webhook nodes stop working after 24 hours unless re-created
The payment provider must use the GET method only
They shared the Test URL, which only works while the editor is listening for a test event
The webhook needs basic authentication enabled before production
objective.explanation: The Test URL is active only while the editor is waiting for a test event. External systems should get the Production URL, which works when the workflow is active or published. Authentication and HTTP method are not the cause here.

objective.question: A Schedule Trigger is set to run at 09:00. The team in Bengaluru sees it run at 14:30 IST every day. What should you fix first?
options: Set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata in Workflow Settings (or set the instance timezone)
Pin the trigger output so it uses IST
Replace the Schedule Trigger with a Webhook
Change the trigger to run every 5.5 hours
objective.explanation: The run is 5 hours 30 minutes late, which matches a UTC timezone. The Schedule Trigger uses the workflow timezone, or the instance timezone if none is set. Setting Asia/Kolkata fixes it. Pinning and interval changes do not fix timezone.

objective.question: You change a published workflow's schedule from 09:00 to 08:00 in the editor. The next day it still runs at 09:00. What most likely happened?
options: The Schedule Trigger ignores hour changes after the first run
The change was not saved and published again, so production still uses the old version
n8n always rounds schedules to the nearest hour
Schedule changes take a week to apply
objective.explanation: Unsaved or unpublished trigger changes do not apply to production. You must save the workflow and publish it again. The other options are not real n8n behaviour.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node returns 25 items. The next node is a Slack node that posts a message. Slack receives 25 separate messages but you wanted one summary. What is the best fix?
options: Use a Switch node to split items into 25 outputs
Change the Schedule Trigger to run once a day
Pin the HTTP Request output
Add an Aggregate node (or a Code node) before Slack to combine the items into one
objective.explanation: Nodes run once per input item by default, so 25 items give 25 messages. Combining items into one with Aggregate or Code gives a single summary. Switch, pinning and schedule changes do not reduce the item count.

objective.question: How many outputs does the IF node have?
options: Exactly two: true and false
Two, plus an optional fallback output
As many as the rules you define
One output, plus an error output
objective.explanation: The IF node has exactly two outputs, true and false. Multiple outputs with an optional fallback describe the Switch node.

objective.question: You route support tickets by priority with a Switch node: High, Medium and Low. Some tickets arrive with an empty priority field and silently disappear. What should you do?
options: Pin the data so empty priorities get a default
Use a Merge node before the Switch
Enable the Switch node's fallback output and connect it to a handling branch
Replace the Switch with an IF node
objective.explanation: Items that match no rule are dropped unless you use the fallback output. Turning it on and connecting it catches unmatched items. IF only has two outputs and pinning affects test runs only.

objective.question: You pinned the output of an HTTP Request node while building a workflow. You then publish the workflow on a schedule. What data does the scheduled production run use?
options: The pinned data for the first run only
No data; pinned nodes are skipped in production
Live data fetched by the HTTP Request node
The pinned data, until you unpin it
objective.explanation: Pinned data affects test runs in the editor only. Production executions always run the node and fetch live data.

objective.question: Your manager asks for proof that last night's scheduled run actually happened, without you running it again. Where do you look?
options: The pinned data panel
The Schedule Trigger's parameter panel
The workflow's version history
The Executions list for the workflow
objective.explanation: Production executions are recorded in the Executions list with time and status. Pinned data and parameters show configuration, not run history.

objective.question: One branch gives customer records and another gives order records. Both have a customer_id field. You want one item per customer with their order details added. Which node fits best?
options: Merge node, combining by matching fields
Schedule Trigger
Switch node
IF node
objective.explanation: The Merge node can combine items from two inputs by matching a field such as customer_id. IF and Switch route items; they do not join data.

objective.question: An API returns items with 30 fields. You need only name, email and a new field status = "new" before sending to a CRM. Which approach is cleanest?
options: Use Merge in Append mode
Use Edit Fields (Set) to set the three fields and keep only the set fields
Pin the data with only the three fields
Use a Switch node with three outputs
objective.explanation: Edit Fields (Set) can add or change fields and drop all others. Switch and Merge do not reshape fields, and pinning only affects tests.

objective.question: In an Edit Fields node, you want a field to hold the value of the "title" field from the current input item. Which expression is correct?
options: {{ $input.title }}
{{ $json.title }}
{{ $node.title }}
{{ title }}
objective.explanation: $json refers to the JSON of the current item, so {{ $json.title }} reads its title field. The other forms are not valid ways to read the current item's field.

objective.question: A workflow with a Webhook node is published. An external system calls a URL containing "/webhook-test/" and gets an error saying the webhook is not registered. The workflow itself is fine. What is the fix?
options: Click 'Listen for test event' and leave the editor open permanently
Change the HTTP method to POST
Unpublish and republish the workflow
Give the external system the Production URL, which uses a different path
objective.explanation: The "/webhook-test/" path is the Test URL, which works only while the editor listens. A published workflow is reached through the Production URL. Keeping the editor open is not a production solution.

objective.question: On a self-hosted n8n instance with no workflow timezone set, which setting decides the timezone the Schedule Trigger uses?
options: The instance timezone, set with the GENERIC_TIMEZONE environment variable
Always UTC, with no way to change it
The timezone of the API you call
The browser's timezone of whoever saved the workflow
objective.explanation: If the workflow has no timezone in Workflow Settings, n8n uses the instance timezone, set by GENERIC_TIMEZONE on self-hosted. Browser and API timezones do not control the schedule.

objective.question: You want a workflow to run whenever a new issue is opened in a GitHub repository, without writing your own webhook handling. What should you use as the trigger?
options: Schedule Trigger every second
An HTTP Request node at the start
The GitHub app trigger node for that event
Manual Trigger
objective.explanation: App trigger nodes start a workflow on events in a service, such as a new GitHub issue. Manual Trigger does not run in production, and HTTP Request is not a trigger.

subjective.question: Explain the main trigger types in n8n and when you would use each one.
subjective.answer: Every workflow starts with a trigger node. The Manual Trigger lets me run the workflow by clicking in the editor. I use it only for building and testing, because it never runs in production. The Schedule Trigger runs the workflow at fixed times or intervals, for example every day at 9 AM IST. I use it for reports, syncs and clean-up jobs. The Webhook node gives a URL that an external system can call, so the workflow runs the moment an event happens, such as a form submission. App trigger nodes, like those for GitHub, Gmail or Google Sheets, start the workflow on events inside a specific service without me building the webhook logic. For any unattended run, I need Schedule, Webhook or an app trigger, and the workflow must be active or published.
keyPoints: Manual Trigger is for testing only and never runs in production
Schedule Trigger for time-based jobs
Webhook for event-driven calls from external systems
App triggers for service-specific events
Unattended runs need an active or published workflow

subjective.question: What is the difference between the Webhook Test URL and Production URL? Describe a bug this difference causes.
subjective.answer: A Webhook node shows two URLs. The Test URL works only while the editor is listening for a test event, after I click to listen. It lets me send a sample request and see the data in the editor. The Production URL works only when the workflow is active or published, and it runs without the editor open. The two URLs have different paths, so they are not interchangeable. A common bug is copying the Test URL into an external system like a payment gateway or form tool. It works while I am testing, so it looks fine. Later, when the editor is closed, every call fails. The fix is to publish the workflow and give the external system the Production URL. I check this every time I hand a webhook to another team.
keyPoints: Test URL works only while the editor is listening
Production URL works only when the workflow is active or published
The two URLs are different
Common bug: giving the Test URL to an external system
Fix: publish and share the Production URL

subjective.question: How does n8n process items between nodes, and why does it matter when building workflows?
subjective.answer: Data moves between nodes as a list of items. Each item is a JSON object. By default, a node runs once for each input item. So if an HTTP Request node returns 50 records, the next node processes 50 items. For a Slack or email node, this means 50 messages. This is useful when I want per-record actions, such as creating one CRM contact per row. It is a problem when I want a single summary. In that case I combine the items first, using an Aggregate node, a Code node, or Edit Fields with suitable expressions, so only one item reaches the sending node. Understanding items also helps with expressions: $json refers to the current item. Many beginner bugs, like duplicate messages, come from forgetting per-item execution.
keyPoints: Data flows as a list of JSON items
Nodes run once per input item by default
Many items into Slack or email means many messages
Use Aggregate, Code or Edit Fields to build one summary
$json refers to the current item

subjective.question: Walk through how you would build a scheduled workflow that fetches data from an API and posts a daily summary to Slack.
subjective.answer: I start with a Schedule Trigger set to, say, every day at 9:00, and I set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata in Workflow Settings. Next, an HTTP Request node calls the API, with authentication stored in a credential, not hard-coded. I run it once and pin the output so I can build the rest without calling the API again. Then I use Edit Fields to keep only the fields I need. Because the API returns many items, I add an Aggregate or Code node to combine them into one item with a summary text. Then a Slack node posts that text to a channel. An IF node can skip posting when there is no data. Finally, I save and publish the workflow, and check the Executions list the next day to confirm it ran on schedule without me opening the editor.
keyPoints: Schedule Trigger with correct timezone
HTTP Request with stored credentials
Pin data while building
Combine items into one summary before Slack
Save, publish, and verify in Executions

subjective.question: A scheduled workflow runs at the wrong time. How do you troubleshoot it?
subjective.answer: First I compare the expected and actual times. If the gap is 5 hours 30 minutes, it is almost certainly a UTC versus IST problem. I open Workflow Settings and check the timezone. If none is set, n8n uses the instance timezone, which on self-hosted comes from the GENERIC_TIMEZONE environment variable. I set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata if the team expects IST. Second, I check that the trigger settings are what I think, such as the hour, the interval or the cron expression. Third, I make sure the change was saved and the workflow published again, because unsaved trigger changes do not reach production. Finally, I look at the Executions list to see actual run times after the fix, so I have evidence that the schedule is correct.
keyPoints: 5h30m gap suggests UTC vs IST
Workflow timezone overrides instance timezone
GENERIC_TIMEZONE on self-hosted
Save and republish after changes
Confirm in the Executions list

subjective.question: Compare the IF node and the Switch node. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: Both nodes route items based on conditions. The IF node has exactly two outputs: true and false. Each item goes down one of them. I use IF for simple yes or no decisions, such as 'is the amount above 10,000' or 'is the list empty'. The Switch node can have many outputs, one per rule or value, plus an optional fallback output for items that match no rule. I use Switch when there are three or more paths, such as routing tickets by High, Medium and Low priority, or by country. Chaining many IF nodes for this becomes hard to read. With Switch, I turn on the fallback output so unexpected values, like an empty priority, are handled instead of silently dropped. Choosing the right one keeps workflows readable and safe.
keyPoints: IF has exactly two outputs: true and false
Switch has many outputs
Switch has an optional fallback output
Use IF for binary decisions, Switch for multiple routes
Fallback prevents silently dropped items

subjective.question: What does the Merge node do, and give two practical uses.
subjective.answer: The Merge node takes items from two or more inputs and brings them together into one stream. It has different modes. The simplest is appending, where items from all inputs are listed one after another. Another is combining, where items are joined, for example by matching a common field like customer_id, or by position. It can also wait for parallel branches and pass on data from one chosen branch. A first practical use: I fetch customers from a CRM and orders from a billing API in two branches, then merge by customer_id to get one item per customer with order details. A second use: after an IF node splits items into two paths for different processing, I merge both paths back so one Slack node sends the final result. I always check the item count after a merge.
keyPoints: Merge combines data from multiple inputs
Append mode lists items together
Combine mode joins by matching field or position
Use to join data from two sources
Use to rejoin branches after IF or Switch

subjective.question: What is data pinning in n8n? Explain its benefits and its limits.
subjective.answer: Pinning saves a node's output in the editor so later test runs reuse that data instead of executing the node again. I usually pin the trigger or an HTTP Request node after one good run. The benefits are clear: I do not call a paid or rate-limited API repeatedly, I get the same input each time, which makes debugging easier, and I can test webhook-based logic without sending a new request every time. I can also edit pinned data to test edge cases like an empty list. The key limit is that pinned data affects test runs only. Production executions always run the node and fetch live data. So a workflow that works with pinned data may still fail in production if the live data looks different. I test once with live data before publishing.
keyPoints: Pinning stores node output for reuse in test runs
Saves API calls and gives repeatable tests
Pinned data can be edited to test edge cases
Pinned data does not apply in production
Test with live data before publishing

subjective.question: What does activating or publishing a workflow mean, and how do you prove it is working in production?
subjective.answer: A workflow in the editor does not run on its own. To run on its trigger, such as a schedule, webhook or app event, it must be activated. In newer n8n versions, the old Active toggle became a Publish action, but the idea is the same: only the activated or published version runs on triggers. This also means that after I edit a trigger, I must save and publish again, or production keeps using the old version. The workflow also needs a production-capable trigger; a Manual Trigger will never fire. To prove it works, I close the editor and wait for the next scheduled time. Then I open the Executions list and check that a production execution appears with the right time and a success status. I also confirm the output, like the Slack message, actually arrived.
keyPoints: Only activated or published workflows run on triggers
Active toggle became Publish in newer versions
Save and republish after trigger changes
Manual Trigger never runs in production
Prove runs using the Executions list

subjective.question: What is the Edit Fields (Set) node used for? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Edit Fields, earlier called the Set node, adds, changes or removes fields on each item. It is the main tool for shaping data between nodes. For example, an API returns 30 fields but my CRM needs only name, email and phone. I set those fields and choose to keep only the set fields, so the rest is dropped. I can also add new fields, such as status set to 'new' or source set to 'website'. Values can be fixed or built with expressions, like {{ $json.first_name }} plus {{ $json.last_name }} to create a full name, or a formatted date. Shaping data early makes later nodes simpler and reduces errors from unexpected fields. It also makes the data easier to read when I debug in the editor. It still runs per item, so it does not combine items by itself.
keyPoints: Adds, changes or removes fields on items
Option to keep only set fields
Supports fixed values and expressions
Shapes data for downstream nodes
Runs per item; does not aggregate by default

subjective.question: How do you use the HTTP Request node safely and effectively in a production workflow?
subjective.answer: The HTTP Request node calls any REST API, so it covers services that have no dedicated node. I set the method, URL, query parameters, headers and body. For authentication, I use n8n credentials instead of pasting API keys into the node, so secrets stay out of the workflow JSON. If the API documentation gives a cURL command, I can import it to fill the node quickly. I check how the response is returned; a JSON array usually becomes many items, which affects the next nodes. For large APIs, I use the node's pagination options instead of building loops by hand, and I respect rate limits. I think about failures too: the node can be set to retry or continue on error, so one bad call does not silently break a daily report. Then I pin one good response for building.
keyPoints: Configure method, URL, parameters, headers and body
Store secrets in credentials
Import cURL to set up quickly
Arrays become multiple items
Use pagination, retries and error settings

subjective.question: A Webhook-triggered workflow needs to send back a custom response to the caller. What options does the Webhook node give for responding?
subjective.answer: The Webhook node has a setting that controls when and how it responds to the caller. It can respond immediately, which tells the caller the request was received while the workflow keeps running. This is good when the caller has a short timeout or does not need results. It can respond when the last node finishes, returning the data from the final node, which suits short, quick workflows. The third option is to respond using a separate Respond to Webhook node, which lets me choose exactly what to send back, such as a custom JSON body, status code or headers, at a specific point in the flow. For example, I can validate input with an IF node and send a 400 error on the false branch. I choose based on how long the workflow takes and what the caller expects.
keyPoints: Respond immediately for quick acknowledgement
Respond when last node finishes to return results
Respond to Webhook node for custom body, status and headers
Choose based on caller timeouts and needs
Can return errors from specific branches

subjective.question: Some app trigger nodes use webhooks and others poll. Explain the difference and why it matters.
subjective.answer: An app trigger can work in two ways. A webhook-based trigger registers a URL with the service, and the service calls n8n the moment the event happens, for example a new GitHub issue. This is fast and efficient. A polling trigger does not wait for a call; n8n checks the service on an interval, such as every minute or every hour, and starts the workflow if it finds new data. Some services do not offer webhooks, so polling is the only choice, for example certain spreadsheet or email triggers. This matters for design. Polling adds delay up to the interval and uses API calls even when nothing changed, which can hit rate limits. Webhook triggers are near real-time but need the n8n instance to be reachable from the internet, which matters for self-hosted setups behind a firewall.
keyPoints: Webhook triggers receive calls from the service
Polling triggers check on an interval
Polling adds delay and uses API calls
Some services only support polling
Webhooks need a publicly reachable instance

subjective.question: Your scheduled workflow did not run last night. Give a step-by-step troubleshooting checklist.
subjective.answer: First, I open the Executions list. If there is a failed execution, the schedule worked and I debug the failing node, often an HTTP Request error or an expired credential. If there is no execution at all, the trigger did not fire. Then I check that the workflow is active or published, and that my latest changes were saved and published, since unpublished edits do not apply. Next, I confirm the trigger is a Schedule Trigger and not a Manual Trigger. I check the timezone in Workflow Settings and the instance timezone, because the run may have happened at a different hour than expected. On self-hosted, I check that the n8n instance or container was actually running at that time. Finally, after fixing, I watch the next scheduled run in Executions to confirm.
keyPoints: Check Executions list first
Failed run versus no run tells you where to look
Confirm workflow is published with latest changes
Check trigger type and timezone
On self-hosted, confirm the instance was running

subjective.question: An API returns 40 records and you need one email containing a summary of all of them. How do you build this in n8n?
subjective.answer: Because nodes run once per input item, sending the 40 items straight to an email node would send 40 emails. So I combine them first. One option is the Aggregate node, which collects a field, or all item data, into a single item holding a list. After that, an Edit Fields node or an expression can turn the list into readable text, for example joining titles with line breaks. Another option is a Code node, where I loop over all input items in JavaScript and return one item with a formatted summary, such as counts and totals. Before combining, I usually use Edit Fields to keep only the fields I need. Then the email or Slack node receives one item and sends one message. I test with pinned data, then check one live production run.
keyPoints: Per-item execution would send 40 emails
Aggregate node combines items into one
Code node can build a custom summary
Format text with Edit Fields or expressions
Only one item should reach the send node

steps.overview: This step explains how data moves through an n8n workflow. Data travels as a list of items, and each item holds JSON. You will learn to read that data with expressions, reshape it with looping, splitting and aggregating nodes, and drop into the Code node when no built-in node fits. Level 1 and Level 2 knowledge checks test these ideas heavily, and they are the base for every real workflow you build.
objectives: Describe the n8n item structure (an array of objects with a json key and an optional binary key) and how nodes process items.
Write expressions with {{ $json }} and $('Node Name') to reference fields from the current or any earlier node.
Choose between automatic per-item processing, Loop Over Items, Split Out, Aggregate and Summarize for a given data shape.
Write a Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' and 'Run Once for Each Item' modes that returns valid n8n items.
Transform a CSV of orders into per-customer totals using both a no-code path (Summarize) and a Code node path.

concepts.explanation: An item is the unit of data in n8n. Each node receives and outputs an array of items. Each item is an object with a json key for structured data and an optional binary key for files. For example, a CSV with 50 rows becomes 50 items after parsing.

Most nodes run once for every incoming item automatically. If 50 items reach a Gmail node, it sends 50 emails. This is why you rarely need a manual loop in n8n. The node setting 'Execute Once' forces a node to run only for the first item.

An expression is JavaScript written inside {{ }} in a parameter set to Expression mode. {{ $json.email }} reads a field from the current item of the node's direct input. Expressions can call methods such as {{ $json.name.toUpperCase() }}. They also support n8n helpers like $now and $today (Luxon dates) and $jmespath.

$('Node Name').item.json.field gets the item in that node that is linked to the current item, using paired items. $('Node Name').first(), .last() and .all() give fixed positions or every item. The older $node["Node Name"].json syntax still appears in old workflows. The current $() syntax is the one to learn.

n8n tracks which input item produced each output item. This tracking is what lets .item find the matching item in an earlier node. Built-in nodes keep the links for you. A Code node that builds brand-new items can break them, which causes paired-item errors downstream.

This node splits incoming items into batches of a set size. It sends each batch through the 'loop' output, and when all batches are done it sends the combined results through the 'done' output. Use it for rate limits, very large datasets, or nodes that only process the first item. Do not use it for normal per-item work.

Split Out turns an array field inside one item into many items. Aggregate does the opposite and collects field values from many items into one item. Summarize works like a pivot table: it groups by 'Fields to Split By' and calculates Sum, Count, Average, Min, Max and similar values.

The Code node runs JavaScript or Python when built-in nodes cannot express the logic. 'Run Once for All Items' (the default) gives you every item through $input.all(). 'Run Once for Each Item' runs the code per item and exposes $json. The node must return items, which means objects with a json key.

keyFacts: Data between nodes is always an array of items, and each item looks like { json: {...}, binary?: {...} }.
{{ $json.field }} reads only from the node directly connected before the current one. Use $('Node Name') to read from any earlier node.
$('Node').item uses item linking. Use .first(), .last() or .all() when you need a fixed position or every item.
Code node default mode is 'Run Once for All Items'. $json is only available in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode.
In the Code node, $input.all(), $input.first() and $input.item read the node's input data.
Loop Over Items has two outputs: 'loop' for each batch and 'done' after every batch has been processed.
The Extract From File node parses CSV, XLSX and JSON files from binary data into items. CSV values usually arrive as strings.
On self-hosted n8n, the Code node can use external npm modules or Node built-ins only if they are allowed through NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL or NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN.

pitfalls: Adding Loop Over Items for simple per-item work. Nodes already iterate over every item, so the extra loop only adds complexity.
Forgetting that CSV values are strings. Summing '120' and '80' gives '12080' unless you convert with Number() or set the field type in an Edit Fields (Set) node.
Using $json to read data from a node that is not the direct parent. It silently reads the wrong data; use $('Node Name').item.json instead.
Returning plain values or a single object from the Code node instead of an array of { json: {...} } items. This causes errors or unexpected output.
Building new items in a Code node and then using .item references downstream. This can raise paired-item errors; use .first() or .all(), or keep the item links intact.
Printing an object inside a text expression. It shows [object Object]; use JSON.stringify() or select a specific field.
